column2: How should a critical self-hosted Azure agent upgrade be introduced?
column3: Test a representative workload on updated capacity, then roll out with a recovery option and compatibility checks.

column2: Does an Azure container job eliminate host security responsibility?
column3: No. It requires a compatible agent and container runtime; shared host resources and privileged mounts can weaken isolation.

column2: Why can persistent Azure agent state contaminate later jobs?
column3: Files, caches, processes or credentials can survive and affect another run; use isolation and reliable cleanup.

column2: What authority does an Azure Resource Manager service connection provide?
column3: A way for authorised pipelines to authenticate as an Azure identity whose role assignments determine accessible resources.

column2: How does workload identity federation remove a service connection's client secret?
column3: A trusted external token is exchanged for an Entra access token; federation claims replace possession of a stored client secret.

column2: How does a managed identity differ from a manually credentialled application service principal?
column3: Azure manages its credential lifecycle; an application service principal may otherwise require managed secrets, certificates or federation.

column2: Why distinguish service connection User and Administrator permissions?
column3: Using an existing connection need not permit changing its identity, scope or security configuration.

column2: Does creating an Azure service connection authorise every pipeline to use it?
column3: No. Grant pipeline access explicitly; broad access must be a deliberate choice.

column2: Which Azure pipeline resources commonly need protection from untrusted consumers?
column3: Service connections, environments, agent pools, secure files and secret-bearing variable groups.

column2: Why put Azure deployment checks on the protected resource?
column3: Resource owners control them outside the pipeline YAML, limiting bypass by pipeline editors.

column2: What evidence links an Azure service connection change to its impact?
column3: Audit actor/time/change records, affected connection identity and scope, pipeline runs and target-service activity logs.

column2: How does an Azure deployment job connect execution to deployment history?
column3: It references an environment, recording deployments against that environment or its selected resource.

column2: What does an Azure environment resource identify?
column3: A deployment target, currently a virtual machine or Kubernetes resource; an environment can also record deployments without such resources.

column2: Who determines the approvers for an Azure protected-resource approval check?
column3: The resource administrator configures approvers; the stage waits for the applicable approval before proceeding.

column2: What does an Azure branch control check validate?
column3: That linked resource sources use allowed branches and, if configured, that those branches are protected.

column2: What does an Azure required-template check require of a consuming pipeline?
column3: That it extends from the specified template; merely copying similar steps is insufficient.

column2: What does an Azure business-hours check constrain?
column3: When the stage may start using the protected resource; other checks must also succeed within the permitted window.

column2: What does an Azure exclusive lock protect?
column3: It serialises access to a protected resource; lockBehavior determines sequential processing or keeping the latest run.

column2: Does lockBehavior: sequential make a deployment itself idempotent?
column3: No. It orders competing stages; safe reruns and recovery still require idempotent deployment logic.

column2: When choose an Azure REST check rather than an Azure Monitor alerts check?
column3: Use REST for a custom external decision; use the Monitor check to gate on configured alert status.

column2: How can an Azure environment show which revision reached production?
column3: Follow its deployment history to the pipeline run and associated commits, artifacts and work items.

column2: How do organisation and project security responsibilities differ in Azure DevOps?
column3: Organisation settings govern shared boundaries; project permissions control project resources within those constraints.

column2: Does connecting Azure DevOps to Entra ID automatically grant every directory user repository access?
column3: No. Authentication is integrated, but Azure DevOps membership, access levels and permissions still govern access.

column2: What determines an Azure pipeline job token's effective permissions?
column3: Its job authorisation scope and the permissions of the corresponding project or collection Build Service identity.

column2: Why prefer project-scoped Azure job authorisation where feasible?
column3: It reduces unintended cross-project access compared with collection-scoped authority.

column2: When choose an Azure secure file rather than a variable group?
column3: For a protected file such as a certificate; variable groups share named values, including separately protected secret variables.

column2: Which Azure Artifacts feed roles suit consuming existing packages versus publishing packages?
column3: Feed Reader for existing package consumption; Feed Publisher (Contributor) for publication, subject to the required upstream behaviour.

column2: Why can an Azure user view a resource while a pipeline cannot consume it?
column3: User permissions and pipeline authorisation are separate; the executing build identity and resource checks also matter.

column2: Does the Azure DevOps CLI extension support Azure DevOps Server?
column3: No. It supports Services; use supported Server APIs and matching API versions for on-premises automation.

column2: Which Azure DevOps audit events help investigate weakened repository controls?
column3: Permission and branch-policy changes, correlated with actor, time and affected resource; export for retention beyond service limits.
